title: Array / List
description: Contiguous block of memory storing elements of the same type (static arrays) or arbitrary Python objects (dynamic lists). O(1) random access by index. Python list is dynamic — it doubles capacity when full.
when_to_use: need fast random access by index
when_to_avoid: unknown or highly variable size with memory constraints
need fast membership testing (use set instead)
python_example:
lst = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
lst.append(9)       # O(1)
lst.insert(2, 99)   # O(n)
lst.pop()           # O(1)
lst.pop(0)          # O(n) — slow!
lst[2]              # O(1)

title: Linked List
description: Nodes connected by pointers. Each node stores data and a reference to the next (singly) or both next and previous (doubly) node. No random access — must traverse from head.
when_to_use: frequent insertions/deletions at head or known node
when_to_avoid: simple forward iteration only (array is faster due to cache)
python_note: Python's collections.deque is a doubly-linked list that gives O(1) appendleft/popleft, making it ideal for queues and sliding windows.

title: Stack
description: LIFO (Last-In First-Out) structure. All operations happen at the top: push (add), pop (remove), peek (view top). Models call stacks, expression evaluation, and backtracking.
python_example:
stack = []
stack.append(x)   # push O(1)
stack.pop()       # pop O(1)
stack[-1]         # peek O(1)

title: Queue / Deque
description: FIFO (First-In First-Out) structure. Enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Deque (double-ended queue) supports O(1) insert/delete at both ends.
python_example:
from collections import deque
q = deque()
q.append(x)       # enqueue right O(1)
q.appendleft(x)   # enqueue left O(1)
q.popleft()       # dequeue front O(1)
q.pop()           # dequeue right O(1)

title: Hash Set
description: Unordered collection of unique elements backed by a hash table. Provides average O(1) add, remove, and membership test.
when_to_avoid: need sorted iteration (use sorted list or SortedList)
need to maintain insertion order (use dict in Python 3.7+)
python_example:
seen = set()
seen.add(x)          # O(1)
x in seen            # O(1)
seen.discard(x)      # O(1) no error if missing
A & B                # intersection O(min(|A|,|B|))
A | B                # union O(|A|+|B|)

title: Binary Search Tree (BST)
description: Binary tree where left child < parent < right child. Supports sorted iteration, predecessor/successor, and range queries. Performance degrades to O(n) if unbalanced.
when_to_use: need sorted data with fast insert/delete
variants: Red-Black Tree — self-balancing, looser balance (used in Java TreeMap, Python sortedcontainers)
python_note: Python has no built-in BST. Use sortedcontainers.SortedList for O(log n) insert/delete with sorted iteration.

title: Graph Representations
description: Graphs can be represented as adjacency lists (dict of lists) or adjacency matrices (2D array). Choice affects space and operation complexity.

adjacency_matrix.best_for: dense graphs or when O(1) edge check is critical

when_to_use_list: most graph problems — sparse graphs are common
python_example:
# Adjacency list (default choice)
graph = {0: [(1, 5), (2, 3)], 1: [(3, 1)], ...}

# Defaultdict for cleaner construction
from collections import defaultdict
g = defaultdict(list)
g[u].append((v, weight))

title: Monotone Stack
description: A stack that maintains elements in monotone increasing or decreasing order. When a new element violates the invariant, elements are popped and processed. Used to find next-greater/smaller elements in O(n).
key_insight: Even though there's a nested loop, total push/pop operations across all iterations is O(n) — each element is pushed once and popped once.
code_template:
# Next Greater Element
def next_greater(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    result = [-1] * n
    stack = []  # stores indices
    for i, val in enumerate(arr):
        while stack and arr[stack[-1]] < val:
            idx = stack.pop()
            result[idx] = val
        stack.append(i)
    return result

title: LRU Cache
description: Least Recently Used cache evicts the least recently accessed item when capacity is full. Implemented with a hash map (O(1) lookup) + doubly linked list (O(1) move-to-front and eviction).
key_insight: Hash map stores key → node pointer. Doubly linked list maintains access order (most recent at head, least recent at tail). On access: move node to head. On eviction: remove tail node.
python_example:
from functools import lru_cache

# Built-in LRU cache decorator
@lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def expensive_fn(x): ...

# Or collections.OrderedDict for manual implementation

title: Bloom Filter
description: Space-efficient probabilistic data structure for membership testing. Can have false positives (says 'maybe in set' when not) but never false negatives (says 'not in set' when it is). Uses multiple hash functions and a bit array.

complexity.insert: O(k) where k = number of hash functions
complexity.space: O(m) bits (much smaller than exact set)

when_to_use: avoid expensive disk/network lookups for clearly-absent items
database query optimisation (avoid reading disk for non-existent keys)
when_to_avoid: deletions required (standard bloom filters don't support delete)
zero false positives required (use exact set)

title: Treap / Skip List
description: Treap: BST + random priorities maintaining heap property — self-balancing with high probability. Skip list: layered linked list with O(log n) search via express lanes. Both give O(log n) operations with simpler implementation than AVL/red-black trees.
when_to_use: competitive programming where balanced BST is needed
concurrent data structures (skip lists are more lock-friendly)
when implementation simplicity matters over constant factors
